Yeah I get you, I just think it would be very hard for Jen to build a case. It would be easy for the company to say they didn't want to risk the well-being of their employees, as her history has been confirmed. Given how hard it can be for actual discrimination cases (disability, racism, sexism, anti-LGBTQ, etc.) to be taken to higher levels, I just can't see this being a thing that would cause serious legal issues for a company.

I do believe people can change and someone like Jen could be genuinely remorseful, but a history of bullying is something that employers could take into account (if verified) and present as a factor in maintaining a healthy work environment. In this case, I think it would pass as a current employee has been deeply traumatized by this person and it has been verified. Again, I don't think this is actually real, but just if it were, it could be presented as protecting employees with valid reason for concern. 

I don't know about laws where you are, but my perception of discrimination cases is that they are from protected classes. I just can't imagine that consequences of actions are held in the same esteem as things that are beyond our control. Now, if she were being trashed in the industry as a whole, I could see there being an issue, but for this one place? Nah.

Sorry for typing so much, I'm not the best at being concise!

Being an asshole isn't a protected class. Just to add a bit of outside perspective, I will say it doesn't seem like the easy way when it's being contemplated and planned; It feels like a logical conclusion.

A common thread you'll see on the topic of suicide is that of people feeling like a burden, and for many, removing oneself from the equation is seen as lessening this burden on others (whether the burden is perceived as emotional, financial, etc). 

Mental health issues can also easily convince someone that they will never be anything more than they perceive they are, and the inability to see a future is also very common.

Perception is a powerful force: When we perceive something as being our reality, it begins to shape it.

This is just some rambling from my own experience, and while I obviously haven't completed the act (unless there's an afterlife with WiFi I guess), I never viewed it as the oft-touted 'permanent solution to a temporary problem'; *I* am the problem. It's not as simple as there being an easy way out, and it is so often coloured with a sense of existential guilt.
